title: Relative Clauses — Defining vs. Non-Defining, Whose & Prepositions
subtitle: Add essential or extra information to a noun, and know when commas matter.
objectives: Tell the difference between defining (essential) and non-defining (extra) relative clauses
Use commas correctly with non-defining clauses, and never with defining ones
Use relative clauses with prepositions in both an informal and a formal style

content.intro: You already know who, which and that from A2. At B1, the key question is: does the relative clause tell you which one, or does it just add an extra fact about something already identified?

rules.heading: a) Defining relative clauses (essential information)
rules.body:
No commas. The clause tells you exactly which person or thing is meant — remove it, and the sentence loses essential meaning. That is allowed here (as well as who/which).

  • The woman who lives next door is a doctor. (Which woman? The one who lives next door.)
  • The book that I borrowed was excellent. (Which book? The one I borrowed.)

rules.heading: b) Non-defining relative clauses (extra information)
rules.body:
Commas on both sides. The clause adds extra, non-essential detail — remove it, and the sentence still makes complete sense. That is never used here — only who/which/whose.

  • My sister, who lives in London, is visiting next week. (I have one sister; the clause just adds a fact.)
  • The Eiffel Tower, which was built in 1889, attracts millions of visitors. (There's only one Eiffel Tower — the clause doesn't identify it, just adds information.)

rules.heading: c) Whose (possession)
rules.body:
Use whose to show that something belongs to the person or thing just mentioned — for people and things.

  • That's the man whose car was stolen.
  • It's a company whose products are sold worldwide.

rules.heading: d) Relative clauses with prepositions
rules.body:
Informal (everyday spoken English): preposition stays at the end, and that or nothing is common.

  • She's the woman (that) I told you about.

Formal (written English): preposition moves before whom/which — never before "who" or "that."

  • She's the woman about whom I told you.

examples: The man who called this morning didn't leave his name.
My car, which is ten years old, still runs perfectly.
This is the restaurant that we talked about.
Mr. Silva, whose daughter studies with me, is a professor.
The company I work for is expanding to three new countries.
Paris, which is the capital of France, is famous for its museums.
The person to whom this letter is addressed no longer lives here.
The keys that you were looking for are on the table.

commonMistakes.wrong: My sister that lives in London is visiting.
commonMistakes.right: My sister, who lives in London, is visiting.
commonMistakes.why: "That" is never used in a non-defining clause — use "who"/"which," with commas.

commonMistakes.wrong: The man, who called this morning, didn't leave his name.
commonMistakes.right: The man who called this morning didn't leave his name.
commonMistakes.why: This clause identifies which man — it's defining, so no commas.

commonMistakes.wrong: The woman who's car was stolen is my neighbor.
commonMistakes.right: The woman whose car was stolen is my neighbor.
commonMistakes.why: "Whose" shows possession; "who's" is short for "who is" — they sound the same but mean different things.

commonMistakes.wrong: She's the woman about that I told you.
commonMistakes.right: She's the woman that I told you about. / She's the woman about whom I told you.
commonMistakes.why: A preposition can go before "whom" (formal) or stay at the end with "that"/nothing (informal) — never directly before "that."

commonMistakes.wrong: I have two sisters who live in London.
commonMistakes.right: (only correct if you actually have more than one sister living in London — otherwise: My sister, who lives in London, is visiting.)
commonMistakes.why: Whether you use commas changes the meaning: without commas, it implies you have several sisters and this identifies which ones.

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with who, which, that, or whose (more than one may be possible for the defining clauses).

items.prompt: The car ___ I bought last year has already broken down.
items.explanation: Defining clause about a thing — that or which both work.

items.prompt: My father, ___ worked as an engineer for thirty years, just retired.
items.explanation: Non-defining clause about a person — only "who" (never "that").

items.prompt: That's the boy ___ bicycle was stolen last week.
The hotel ___ we stayed at was surprisingly cheap.
London, ___ I visited last summer, is an amazing city.
items.explanation: Non-defining clause about a place — only "which" (never "that").

items.prompt: The woman ___ answered the phone was very polite.

items.incorrect: My brother that lives in Canada is a doctor.
answer: My brother, who lives in Canada, is a doctor.
items.explanation: Non-defining clause (he has one brother) — needs "who" and commas, not "that."

items.incorrect: The man, who I met yesterday, works at the bank.
answer: The man who I met yesterday works at the bank.
items.explanation: This clause identifies which man — it's defining, so no commas.

items.incorrect: She's the girl who's phone I borrowed.
answer: She's the girl whose phone I borrowed.

items.incorrect: This is the topic about that we spoke.
answer: This is the topic that we spoke about.
This is the topic about which we spoke.
items.explanation: A preposition never goes directly before "that" — put it at the end (informal) or before "which"/"whom" (formal).

exercises.title: Guided Production
exercises.instructions: Write your own sentence for each prompt. There's no single correct answer — a model answer is shown for comparison after you submit.

items.prompt: Write one sentence with a defining relative clause (using who, which or that) about a person you know.
items.modelAnswer: The friend who helped me move last month lives just around the corner.

items.prompt: Write one sentence with a non-defining relative clause (using who or which, with commas) about your hometown or a famous place.
items.modelAnswer: My hometown, which is famous for its beaches, gets very crowded in the summer.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using whose to describe someone's possession.
items.modelAnswer: I work with someone whose brother is a professional football player.

summary: Defining clauses (no commas) tell you which one; that/who/which are all possible.
Non-defining clauses (with commas) add extra information; only who/which — never that.
Whose shows possession, for people and things.
A preposition can go before whom/which (formal) or stay at the end with that/nothing (informal) — never directly before that.
